articles.title: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is in Peru as part of his Latin America tour, just weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.

The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.

The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.

"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago .

Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began.

"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.

Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.

Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.

Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.

The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.

They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.

For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.

"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.

The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.

The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.

Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.

But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.

Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.

But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.

"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.

And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.

"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.

"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."

Who is Robert Prevost, the new Pope Leo XIV?

Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.

Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.

Father Miranda also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.

"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".

That unity has been on display in the run up to the Mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.

Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.

Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.

But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass.

Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.

Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.

"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

articles.title: Conservative Party pays artist for Burnham images after legal threat
articles.summary: Stanley Chow had threatened to sue the Conservative Party for using his illustrations of the PM.
articles.body:
The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minister.

Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture - which Burnham has used on social media - without permission.

He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. It is understood the Tories agreed to pay a £1,000 fee for use of the image - and contributed an unknown sum to Chow's legal fees.

The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler".

Chow posted on Facebook: "The Conservative Party have settled after their recent indiscretion of using my image without my permission."

He added: "Maybe ask first… admittedly I would have said no, but it would have been a damn sight cheaper for the Tory Party if they just hired any illustrator to do their take on a cartoon of Burnham… hopefully this a lesson learned. Copyright matters."

A Conservative spokesman said: "The Conservative Party values the importance of intellectual property in the creative industries. We consider this matter closed."

Manchester United fan Chow, a Labour supporter, has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho.

He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city.

He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager.

articles.title: Nick Cannon tried putting all six mothers of his 12 children into one group chat to coordinate Thanksgiving, but the comedian now says the experiment quickly became chaotic and is not something he plans to repeat
articles.summary: You would understand what it feels like to put 12 of your children and six of their mamas in one group chat.
articles.body: You would understand what it feels like to put 12 of your children and six of their mamas in one group chat. Probably not, but Nick Cannon does, and he is not particularly happy about how it turned out.The comedian recently revealed that his attempt to bring all six mothers of his children together in one group chat to coordinate Thanksgiving plans quickly went off the rails. What was supposed to make holiday planning easier apparently turned into an experience he would rather not repeat.Speaking on the 'On Par with Maury Povich' podcast on November 9, Cannon opened up about the short-lived group chat during a segment called 'On Par or Off the Rails'. When host Maury Povich asked him whether bringing all six mothers together in one chat to figure out Thanksgiving logistics was a good idea, Cannon admitted that he had already tried it."Tried it," he said, describing the experience as "off the rails" and "too wild for TV".Well, so much for making holiday planning a little easier.Nick Cannon says the six mothers are civil with each otherPovich also asked Cannon whether the mothers of his children get along with one another. The comedian responded with a question of his own, joking, "How do you define get along?"He then clarified that the women are civil with one another, adding that "everybody has their own life". However, bringing everyone together in a single group chat was apparently a different matter."Putting them all in a group chat together? Not the best idea," he admitted.Cannon's response did not mean that the women had fallen out or that there was a major dispute going on. Rather, maintaining a civil relationship and communicating together as one large group are two very different things.Who are the six mothers of Nick Cannon's 12 children?For those unfamiliar with Cannon's family tree, the television host shares 12 children with six women. He welcomed his first children, twins Moroccan and Monroe, with singer Mariah Carey in 2011. The former couple married in 2008 and finalised their divorce in 2016.He later welcomed three children with model Brittany Bell: son Golden, daughter Powerful and son Rise. With DJ Abby De La Rosa, he shares twins Zion and Zillion, along with daughter Beautiful.Cannon also has a son, Legendary, with model Bre Tiesi, and a daughter, Onyx, with photographer LaNisha Cole.With Alyssa Scott, he welcomed son Zen and daughter Halo. Zen sadly died at five months old in December 2021 after being diagnosed with brain cancer.The six women, therefore, are Mariah Carey, Brittany Bell, Abby De La Rosa, Bre Tiesi, LaNisha Cole and Alyssa Scott, all of whom were part of the group chat Cannon discussed on the podcast.Bre Tiesi has spoken about the family's complicated dynamicsCannon's comments also come amid earlier conversations about how the different households navigate their relationships with one another. Bre Tiesi, who shares son Legendary with the comedian, has previously also spoken about her efforts to build relationships with the other mothers.During an appearance on E!'s 'Hot Goss', Tiesi said she would like the children to have close relationships with their siblings but acknowledged that relationships between the mothers could be difficult."I would love to embrace the more, but the relationships with the mothers are, unfortunately, too difficult to do so," she said.She also explained that Cannon had a great role to play in creating an environment where the children could maintain those sibling relationships."I'm just going to remove myself so that the children can have the best relationship," Tiesi said, adding that Cannon needed to step up and support the children.Nick Cannon's family life could get its own Netflix seriesThere may soon be more to learn about how Cannon manages his large family. During the conversation with Povich, the comedian also teased his upcoming Netflix docuseries, which is expected to explore his family life and relationships.When Povich asked whether any of the mothers get upset about him spending more time with some than others, Cannon jokingly replied, "It sounds like you've seen my docuseries already."The project is expected to offer a closer look at a family arrangement that has attracted considerable public attention over the years.For now, however, Cannon seems to have learnt at least one lesson about managing it all: some conversations are probably better kept out of a single group chat.You use AI every day. articles.summary: JAIPUR: More than 26 lakh of the 41.65 lakh voters deleted by Election Commission of India (ECI) in Rajasthan's draft SIR are still listed on State
articles.body: JAIPUR: More than 26 lakh of the 41.65 lakh voters deleted by Election Commission of India (ECI) in Rajasthan's draft SIR are still listed on State Election Commission (SEC) electoral rolls prepared for 2026 Panchayati Raj and urban local body polls, an analysis by People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL), dated Nov 11, has found. The data studied includes SEC's second panchayat rolls supplement published up to Oct 12.The findings have raised concerns about the accuracy and integrity of the electoral rolls in several districts. PUCL's district-wise assessment showed Baran has the highest share of ECI-deleted voters still appearing on SEC rolls at 83.1%, followed by Pali (81.8%), Jalore (81.5%), Bikaner (81.4%), Sirohi (80.5%) and Deedwana-Kuchaman (80.2%).The analysis further reported that 3.2 lakh people identified as dead by ECI continued to be on SEC rolls statewide. Banswara recorded the highest proportion at 70.7% (23,185 names), followed by Sirohi at 67.5% (13,165), Baran at 61.4% (11,000), Churu at 55.8% (15,050), Jalore at 54.4% (12,164), Ajmer at 51.1% (18,713) and Bikaner at 50.8% (14,192). PUCL claimed in the seven districts, at least half of those marked dead by ECI continued to have active entries on SEC rolls.The organisation further said that SEC rolls still included more than 17.32 lakh people whom ECI had deleted as shifted, 3.67 lakh classified as untraceable or absent, and over 1.83 lakh identified as already enrolled elsewhere.The updated figure of over 26 lakh SIR-deleted voters appearing on SEC rolls - 13.7 lakh on panchayat rolls and 12.4 lakh on municipal rolls - is 69,343 fewer than the nearly 26.7 lakh names identified in PUCL's earlier analysis based on SEC's Feb 25 panchayat rolls. The count of people identified as dead by ECI but still present on SEC rolls fell by 31,987, from 3,52,382 to 3,20,395.PUCL said the Oct supplement to the panchayat electoral rolls led to the removal of 69,578 ECI-deleted names, including 32,027 recorded as dead. It further said that SEC added 2.3 lakh names to its panchayat rolls, taking the total number of active names across its rolls to 5,47,86,896, which it said was 32,72,934 (6.4%) more than ECI's final SIR roll of 5,15,13,962. PUCL said the gap in its previous analysis was 30,42,248 (5.9%).SEC secretary Rajesh Verma said the state roll numbers have increased over the past few months. articles.title: Breakthrough HIV drug sees 18 patent filings, may delay affordable generics
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An unusually high 18 patent applications filed in India for lenacapavir, a breakthrough HIV therapy, have raised concerns that these could
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An unusually high 18 patent applications filed in India for lenacapavir, a breakthrough HIV therapy, have raised concerns that these could prolong market exclusivity, delay affordable generics, keep prices high and restrict patient access. Contesting the move, patient groups and civil society have filed opposition with the regulatory authorities, arguing the applications lack novelty and inventive steps.Lenacapavir, a long-acting injectable, administered twice yearly for both HIV prevention and treatment, a medicine designated as essential by WHO.Last year, US FDA approved Gilead Sciences' lenacapavir as the first and only twice-yearly injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis to reduce sexually acquired HIV. Gilead has filed at least 18 patent pleas till date in India, covering different aspects of it, including the base compound, salt forms, formulations, dosing regimens, compositions, and methods of use."The pattern of filings reflects a systematic strategy to create layered patent protection around a single medicine, with the effect of deterring generic entry and prolonged monopoly control beyond the standard 20-year patent term. Such practices, also referred to as "evergreening", whereby multiple secondary patents covering minor variations in forms, formulations, or used or pursued to extend exclusivity," KM Gopakumar, senior researcher and legal advisor at TWN told TOI.In a letter to the department for promotion of industry and internal trade, patient groups demanded that the patent office must rigorously examine and reject the company's secondary patent applications.Dr Reddy's is one of six generic manufacturers which has signed voluntary licenses with Gilead to manufacture and commercialise lenacapavir across 120 low and lower middle income countries, including India. The generic injection is projected to cost approximately $40 per person annually. So, apart from the voluntary licence holders, no other generics can manufacture and market the drug.Further, the patents, if granted, are set to expire in 2042, 28 years after the first application was filed. "Granting these patents would legitimise Gilead's evergreening strategy," Prathibha Sivasubramanian of Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, told TOI.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin family in Canada seeks $5.5 million for US gene therapy they hope will help their toddler with rare genetic disorder
articles.summary: An Indian-origin family in Canada's Brampton is trying to raise $5.5 million to take their two-year-old son to the United States for a specialized gene
articles.body: An Indian-origin family in Canada's Brampton is trying to raise $5.5 million to take their two-year-old son to the United States for a specialized gene therapy that they hope could transform his life after he was diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder. Mandeep Chandi and his wife Ramandeep are seeking funds for their son, Zorawar, who suffers from Aromatic L-amino Acid Decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency, a rare genetic condition that affects the nervous system and prevents the brain from producing an enzyme needed to make essential neurotransmitters. The disorder affects the production of dopamine and serotonin, chemical messengers that play a crucial role in controlling movement and other bodily functions.At two-and-a-half years old, Zorawar has been unable to achieve basic developmental milestones such as sitting, walking and talking.Ramandeep Kaur, his mother, told CTV News that every day is a challenge for Zorawar. Several times a week, his eyes will stay rolled upward for up to 30 minutes, which is painful for him. And he can't chew food. So he is still on a liquid diet. “Sometimes he is very irritated, cry all the day, and he is not able to — like he can’t say anything about what is going on with him,” Kaur said."He's just in a newborn situation right now, his brain isn't able to get the proper function," his father Mandeep told INSAUGA Canada. "He's not able to walk, talk or sit. He can't do anything, he just sits in his mom's lap 24/7."Mandeep, who moved to Canada from India in 2015, said caring for their son has been an emotionally and financially challenging experience for the family.Family turns to US for gene therapyThe family is hoping to access a treatment called KEBILIDI, a gene therapy approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for patients with AADC deficiency. The treatment, developed for the rare disorder, is administered directly into the brain and is designed to address the underlying genetic problem.According to Boston Children's Hospital, KEBILIDI became the first FDA-approved gene therapy for AADC deficiency. However, the treatment is not approved in Canada.Mandeep believes the therapy could give his son a chance at achieving developmental milestones that have so far remained out of reach.The family says the procedure itself takes approximately eight hours, with potential improvements becoming noticeable over the following months. However, treatment requires specialist assessment, and outcomes cannot be guaranteed.The family had approached Ontario's Ministry of Health seeking funding for treatment outside Canada, but its application was denied.With no other viable option currently available to them, the parents have turned to crowdfunding to raise the money needed to pursue treatment in Boston.$5.5 million fundraising appealThe family has launched a GoFundMe campaign with a target of $5.5 million Canadian dollars. As of November 14, the fundraiser had collected more than $1.5 million, with approximately 29% of its target reached.The family has appealed to the community to support their efforts, saying they want to give their son an opportunity to access treatment that could potentially improve his quality of life.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2016, farmer Olly Birkbeck began transforming 1,200 acres of intensively farmed Norfolk land into a wildlife haven; a decade later, rare butterflies, orchids and birds have returned
articles.summary: Rare butterflies, orchids and birds have returned to 1,200 acres of former farmland in west Norfolk after a ten-year nature restoration project led by
articles.body: Rare butterflies, orchids and birds have returned to 1,200 acres of former farmland in west Norfolk after a ten-year nature restoration project led by local landowner Olly Birkbeck and Natural England. The changes took place at Massingham Heath, part of the Little Massingham Estate. Ten years ago, the land was used for intensive farming and depended heavily on chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Today, the 1,200-acre site, roughly the size of 680 football pitches, has become a rich mix of grassland, wildflowers and scrub. This was reported in a Natural England press release published on 18 June 2026.Among the wildlife that has returned is the dingy skipper butterfly, which had not been seen in the area for 15 years. Botanists and conservation workers have also recorded pyramidal orchids, wasp spiders, oil beetles and more bird species across the estate. "The wildlife response has been remarkable, with the return of species including skylarks, goshawk, hobby, woodlark and stonechat," said John Ebbage, nature recovery manager at Natural England, in the agency's official announcement. "The dingy skipper butterfly, absent from the area for 15 years, has returned, as have wasp spiders, oil beetles and the beautiful pyramidal orchid."Rethinking conventional crop farmingThe project began around 2016, when Birkbeck, owner of the Massingham Estate, started working with Natural England to look at new ways to manage parts of the land. Instead of continuing with traditional crop farming, the team began creating large natural habitats with financial support from Natural England's agri-environment schemes. "I began working with Natural England around ten years ago to rethink how parts of the estate could be managed," Birkbeck said in the Natural England release. "Their support helped us move away from conventional cropping and towards large-scale habitat creation that has restored the landscape closer to its original character." To plan the restored heathland, the team studied old maps and records. Natural England said the original plan was to restore the heath to its former boundaries using Faden's map of Norfolk and first edition Ordnance Survey maps.Hand-collected seeds and local floraInstead of using standard commercial grass seed, the project used seeds from native plants growing in the surrounding area. Ed Cross, a tenant farmer on the nearby Sandringham Estate, led the practical restoration work. According to Natural England, Cross worked with botanists to collect seeds by hand from ancient Norfolk grasslands. They then matched the seeds to the soil and conditions in different parts of Massingham Heath. The team also planted a specially prepared mix of wildflower seeds collected from nearby areas to create grassland suited to the local environment. This careful planting helped bring back several native plants that had disappeared from the farmland. These included rock-rose, wild thyme and field mouse-ear.Conservation grazing keeps habitats openWildflower-rich grassland needs regular care. Without it, fast-growing grasses and scrub can take over and prevent smaller plants from growing. At Massingham Heath, farm animals help manage the land instead of heavy machinery. "The grassland is carefully managed through conservation grazing using Konik ponies, Bagot goats and Tamworth pigs," Ebbage explained in the Natural England announcement. "This helps control invasive species, prevents aggressive plants from dominating, and allows habitats to develop naturally. We have also encouraged the growth of scrub and trees to support a wider range of wildlife." The different animals disturb the ground in different ways. This creates a variety of small habitats where insects, ground-nesting birds and wildflowers can live and grow.Spring bird arrivals and wider landscape linksBird surveys carried out in spring 2026 show that both migrating birds and species that breed locally are making use of the restored grassland and scrub. Along with skylarks, woodlarks, stonechats, hobbies and goshawks, Natural England reported spring visits from whinchats, lesser and greater whitethroats, wheatears, yellow wagtails, quail and ring ouzels. Massingham Heath is also part of a wider nature recovery effort. The Little Massingham Estate forms part of the proposed west Norfolk nature network. This larger project aims to connect existing wildlife areas, create new natural corridors and encourage farming methods that support wildlife across west Norfolk. Natural England explained that connecting separate wildlife habitats allows animals and plants to spread more easily across the countryside. It also helps build stronger wildlife populations that are better able to survive changes in the environment.Documenting seasonal change through artAlongside wildlife surveys, members of the Society of Wildlife Artists have recorded the changes through their artwork. As part of a series of artist residencies organised under the Massingham Heath Project, artists have visited the estate during different seasons. Their work shows how the former crop fields have gradually changed into living heathland. Natural England has highlighted the ten years of work at the Little Massingham Estate as an example of how nature can recover on working farms. The project shows that long-term funding through agri-environment schemes, together with cooperation between farmers, landowners and conservation groups, can help restore wildlife and plant life across English estates.You use AI every day. articles.title: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's no-gift wedding request revealed as West Virginia animal rescue group thanks two guests for a donation, months after the couple's reported $26 million charity contributions
articles.summary: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appear to have given their wedding guests an alternative to the usual tradition of bringing presents, with reports
articles.body: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appear to have given their wedding guests an alternative to the usual tradition of bringing presents, with reports suggesting the couple encouraged friends and family to support charitable organisations instead. The gesture came to light after an animal rescue group in West Virginia publicly acknowledged receiving a contribution from two people who attended the celebrations. According to the Instagram profile (hancockcountyhumanefoundation), the donation offered a glimpse into how the newlyweds approached wedding gifts, with the request reportedly extending beyond their own celebrations. It also follows a series of charitable contributions made by Swift and Kelce in the weeks leading up to their July 3 wedding.Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding gift request surfaces in charity postThe Hancock County Humane Foundation, an animal rescue organisation based in West Virginia, brought attention to the arrangement through a social media post. The group thanked attorney Mike Simon and his wife, Lisa Simon, for making a donation in connection with a wedding they had recently attended.According to the foundation, the couple had asked their guests to contribute to charitable causes rather than purchase traditional wedding presents. Simon and his wife chose the West Virginia organisation as the recipient of their contribution.The foundation also shared a photograph featuring Swift, Kelce and the Simons. Swift appeared in a red top and jeans, while Kelce wore a blue-and-black jacket, shorts and a baseball cap. The photograph accompanied the organisation's acknowledgement of the donation.Couple's wedding request follows $26 million in charitable contributionsThe reported preference for charitable donations is in keeping with the couple's giving in the run-up to their wedding. According to the Associated Press, before their July 3 celebrations, Swift and Kelce reportedly distributed a combined $26 million among charitable organisations across the United States.Their contributions covered several areas, including food assistance, children's healthcare, education, music programmes and animal welfare. The donations reached organisations working in different communities, from New York and Kansas City to Nashville, Pennsylvania and California.Among the recipients was Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which received $2 million from the couple. The programme provides free books to young children, supporting early childhood literacy. Parton subsequently acknowledged the contribution in a video message, expressing her surprise and gratitude for the gift.Other organisations reported among the beneficiaries included City Harvest, Food Bank For NYC, Feeding America, the ASPCA, New York Cares and the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank. Children's Mercy Hospital in Kansas City and Hassenfeld Children's Hospital at NYU Langone were also included. The list extended to education and music initiatives, with Grammy In The Schools, Education Through Music and Musical Mentors among the organisations receiving support.Swift and Kelce's relationship began with an Eras Tour friendship braceletThe couple's wedding came after a relationship that first attracted attention in 2023. Kelce had attended Swift's Eras Tour concert at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, where he attempted to give the singer a friendship bracelet carrying his phone number. His attempt did not go as planned, prompting him to discuss the experience on his podcast, New Heights, which he hosts with his brother Jason Kelce.By September that year, reports of the pair spending time together had begun circulating. Swift subsequently attended a Kansas City Chiefs game, watching from a suite alongside Kelce's mother, Donna. Their appearance together fuelled speculation about their relationship, which became increasingly public over the following months.Kelce also travelled to Argentina in November 2023 to attend one of Swift's Eras Tour performances. During the concert, she altered a lyric in her song 'Karma' to reference the Chiefs player, giving fans another indication of their growing relationship.Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce relationship journey from public appearances to engagementThroughout 2024, the pair continued to support each other's professional commitments. Swift regularly attended Chiefs games, including the team's Super Bowl appearance, while Kelce made a surprise appearance during one of her London Eras Tour concerts. articles.title: A Missouri couple gave their wrecked Lexus and signed title to an unidentified tow-truck driver in 2018; years later it resurfaced with a $6,450 towing bill, but an appeals court ruled they no longer owned the car
articles.summary: A Missouri appeals court has ruled that a couple who handed over their wrecked Lexus and signed the title over to an unidentified tow-truck driver in 2018
articles.body: A Missouri appeals court has ruled that a couple who handed over their wrecked Lexus and signed the title over to an unidentified tow-truck driver in 2018 no longer owned the vehicle, even after it resurfaced years later with a $6,450 towing bill attached. The decision, in Lawrence and Kay E. Keener v. Somerset Apartment Management, LLC, turns on the legal principle of estoppel and the consequences of signing a title transfer, as per report on Justia U.S. Law.The case began when the Keeners’ Lexus was involved in a wreck in 2018. The vehicle was towed, and the couple signed the title over to the tow-truck driver, who was not identified in the court records.Years later, the car resurfaced with a towing bill of $6,450. The Keeners argued that they still owned the vehicle and should not be responsible for the charges, but the appeals court disagreed. Read more about it, as per the report, here:How the dispute startedThe Keeners’ Lexus was wrecked in 2018, and it was towed from the scene. At some point, they signed the title over to the tow-truck driver, effectively transferring ownership of the vehicle. The identity of the tow-truck driver was not established in the court records. This lack of clarity became a central issue in the case, as the Keeners argued that they could not be held responsible for charges related to a vehicle they no longer owned.The Keeners signed the title, but later said they retained an interest in the Lexus. They argued that the towing company could not charge them for storage or other fees related to a car they had already given away.The towing company's positionThe towing company, Somerset Apartment Management, said the Keeners legally owned the car at the time the charges were assessed. It pointed to the fact that the title transfer had not been properly recorded or processed.The company said that the Keeners’ signature on the title did not automatically transfer ownership. It argued that the transfer had to be completed through the proper channels, including notification to the state.The towing company also argued that the Keeners had benefited from the towing and storage services, even if they had intended to give the car away. It said they should not be allowed to avoid the charges simply because they had signed the title over to someone else.What does estoppel mean hereEstoppel is a legal principle that prevents a person from going back on something that he/she previously said or did. Here the Keeners had given the title to the tow-truck driver, which meant they had given up ownership.The appeals court applied that principle to the facts it had. The court found that the Keeners' conduct, including signing the title, was sufficient to show that they had abandoned ownership of the Lexus.That allowed the towing company to pursue them for charges related to the vehicle, even when the Keeners said they weren’t owners any more. The court saw the signed title as a clear indication of intent to transfer ownership.Why the Keeners lost their court caseThe appeals court zeroed in on the fact that the Keeners had signed the title to the tow-truck driver. It considered this to be a clear act of transfer of ownership, irrespective of whether the transfer was formally recorded.The court also said the Keeners didn’t act quickly to retrieve the vehicle or contest the charges. The delay hurt their case and made it harder to argue they still had an interest in the car.The towing bill of $6,450 was found to be a legitimate charge for services rendered. The court ruled that the Keeners could not escape liability on these charges merely because their intent was to give the car away.What it means for car-ownersThis case shows the importance of knowing what it means to sign over a vehicle title. Once a title is signed, the legal ownership may be considered transferred, even if the new owner is not immediately identified.Vehicle owners should be cautious of working with tow-truck drivers or other third parties. So if you buy a title and the car gets ticketed or gets into more trouble you could be in some serious legal trouble.The decision also suggests that courts can use estoppel to stop a party from backing out of a transaction to which it has already agreed. In this case, the Keeners’ signature on the title was enough to establish that they had given up ownership.A lesson in legal liabilityThe Keeners’ experience serves as a cautionary tale for anyone dealing with a vehicle that’s been wrecked or towed.It is important to know the legal implications of signing a title and to make sure the transfer is properly documented.The case also shows that towing companies might have a strong legal case to prosecute charges, even if the car owner believes that they have given away the car. The key is whether the transfer of ownership was legally effective.Now the Keeners are left with a $6,450 tow bill. For others, it is a reminder that legal ownership is not always as simple as it seems.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 1 stenographer, 4,500 cases: HC seeks explanation over delay in pronouncing order
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi High Court has directed its registry to seek explanations from a trial court judge, the chief judicial magistrate (CJM) and the district
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi High Court has directed its registry to seek explanations from a trial court judge, the chief judicial magistrate (CJM) and the district judge concerned over the failure to pronounce an order that was pending since April 22, 2026.Taking note of the remarks in the trial court's order sheets, Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora sought clarification on the staff shortage and backlog of over 4,500 cases, which were cited to explain the delay.The matter stems from a petition filed by Pradeep Bansal and others under Article 227 of the Constitution, seeking time-bound disposal of an application dated April 8, 2024. The application seeks vacation of an interim stay granted on Dec 1, 2023, in a domestic violence complaint pending before a judicial magistrate, first class, in north Delhi.Justice Arora noted that arguments on the application were completed on Jan 6, 2026, but the trial court was yet to pronounce its order. The matter has remained pending for pronouncement since April 22 and has been deferred four times, most recently on Oct 27.After examining the trial court's order sheets, the high court observed that they did not disclose any clear reason for the prolonged delay. What particularly caught the judge's attention, however, were repeated references to administrative constraints in the trial court's proceedings.One of the order sheets recorded: "This court is working with only one stenographer and having pendency of more than 4,500 cases."Noting that the remark appeared in the order sheet and was followed by similar observations in subsequent orders, Justice Arora sought an explanation from the CJM and the district judge on the circumstances in which these remarks were made. They have been asked to clarify the staffing situation and the extent of case pendency in that court.The trial judge, meanwhile, has been asked to explain why the order has not been pronounced when arguments were concluded in Jan. The registry has been directed to obtain reports from all three judicial authorities, covering both the reasons for the delay and the administrative constraints cited, two days before the next hearing on Dec 3.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A mother left her £1.1 million estate entirely to her son after accusing her daughter of failing to show 'love and respect'; the daughter took the dispute to court and lost
articles.summary: A daughter who was excluded from her mother's £1.1 million estate over allegations that she failed to show enough 'love and respect' has lost her legal
articles.body: A daughter who was excluded from her mother's £1.1 million estate over allegations that she failed to show enough 'love and respect' has lost her legal battle against her brother. Dervishe Halil, who died aged 94 in 2021, left her entire fortune to her eldest son, Dogan Halil, after changing her will several times following a bitter family dispute. Her daughter, Aysel Gencay, challenged the 2018 will, claiming her brother had influenced their mother into disinheriting her. However, a judge rejected the allegations, finding no evidence of undue influence and ruling that the final will was valid, leaving the entire estate to Dogan.What led to the £1.1 million inheritance dispute between siblingsAccording to The Sun, Dervishe Halil moved to London from Cyprus with her husband in 1952. She died in 2021 at the age of 94, leaving behind an estate valued at £1.1 million.Initially, her fortune was intended to be divided among all her children. However, following a disagreement between her eldest son, Dogan, and her daughter, Aysel, Dervishe changed her estate plans. Over four years, she made several separate wills, eventually deciding to leave everything to Dogan, who was 74 at the time of the court proceedings.The family dispute centred on allegations made by Aysel that her brother had taken possession of part of the family's property for his own benefit. She accused him of 'slicing off' a section of the property, an allegation that subsequently became a significant part of the inheritance dispute.Why did a mother threaten to disinherit her daughter over a family feudThe conflict escalated in 2015 when Aysel received a handwritten letter from her mother. The letter warned that she could be excluded from the will unless she apologised, reconciled with Dogan and demonstrated greater affection and respect towards her mother.In the letter, Dervishe criticised Aysel and her other son, Attila, over their treatment of Dogan. She wrote: "Your actions have destroyed my life and home; your actions towards your brother Dogan are very bad and shameful – we saw nothing but goodness from Dogan to all of us."Three years later, Dervishe acted on her warning and excluded Aysel and Attila from her will. In a side letter accompanying the new arrangements, she explained that neither child had fulfilled the conditions she had previously set out. According to The Sun, Dervishe wrote: "Aysel and Attila: None of the conditions in the letter I sent three years ago were fulfilled."She continued: "Unfortunately, nothing has changed. "You still do not talk to your brother Dogan, and you still do not show me love and respect. You destroyed my home, and I deleted you from my will."Her final will, made in 2018, left the entire estate to Dogan. The decision prompted Aysel to bring legal proceedings against her brother, who was responsible for administering the estate.Why did a daughter challenge her mother's £1.1 million will in courtAysel challenged the 2018 will at Central London County Court, alleging that Dogan had influenced their mother and turned her against her. She argued that he had pressured Dervishe into changing her inheritance arrangements and preventing her from receiving a share of the estate.Her legal team argued that the will should be declared invalid because Dervishe either did not properly understand or approve its contents or had been subjected to undue influence. They also raised allegations of fraudulent calumny against Dogan.Aysel's barrister, Peter John, argued that her mother's previous approach to inheritance had been based on treating her children equally. He told the court:"The deceased had always indicated that she would deal with her estate based on equality – informed by her cultural and religious background and her consistent approach towards her children throughout their lives."He also argued that the final will was inconsistent with the relationship Aysel had enjoyed with her mother."The deceased’s purported last will – the 2018 will – was, therefore, a shock to the claimant as the deceased’s only daughter, completely at odds with these statements, and also inconsistent with the relationship which she enjoyed with the deceased throughout her life."What evidence did a daughter present in her £1.1 million inheritance disputeAysel's lawyers also questioned the two handwritten letters, arguing that Dervishe would not have been able to compose them without significant assistance. They pointed to similarities between the language used in the letters and the language used by Dogan.Aysel, who lives in Turkey, maintained that she had remained close to her mother. Giving evidence, she told the court that she regularly travelled from Istanbul to visit Dervishe during her final years. "I remained extremely close to my mother all my life," she said.Her brother Attila was also involved in the proceedings as a co-defendant, alongside Dogan's wife, Susan, who was a fellow executor. Attila had received a one-third share of the estate through a deed of variation made by Dogan and Susan.Why did a judge reject a daughter's £1.1 million inheritance claimAfter considering the evidence, Judge Mark Raeside KC ruled in Dogan's favour, rejecting Aysel's allegations of dishonesty and undue influence. The judge described Dogan as a 'dutiful son' who had done his best for his ageing mother. He also found that Dogan had no involvement in preparing the 2018 will or the accompanying side letters.Judge Raeside said: "I reject the assertion that the deceased had any assistance from Dogan with her will. The evidence makes clear he was simply a dutiful son."Both side letters were written in Turkish in the deceased’s hand, Dogan did not help her and had nothing whatever to do with them."The judge also rejected Aysel's allegations that Dogan had acted dishonestly in relation to the family's property and finances. He said her belief that her brother had taken part of the basement property in Packington Street, Islington, had influenced her view of him over the years.Why did a court uphold a mother's £1.1 million will in favour of her sonThe court heard that Dervishe had attended her solicitor independently when preparing her will. Her solicitor recorded that she appeared mentally sharp and understood what she was doing. When asked why she wanted to exclude her other children, Dervishe reportedly said they were 'not visiting her and not showing any interest'.The judge also rejected the argument that Dervishe lacked testamentary capacity. Although she displayed symptoms of dementia by 2020, he found that she was of sound mind when she made her final will in 2018.In dismissing the case, Judge Raeside said: "Aysel was wrong in her approach. She became fixated on this matter, and her conduct was fundamentally wrong. She raised these matters quite wrongly."He added: "There was no dishonesty by Dogan. Dogan wasn’t responsible for any suspicion, and therefore the case should be dismissed."The judge further stated that Dogan had correctly accounted for the relevant finances and that the allegations against him were misplaced. The court ultimately dismissed Aysel's claims and ruled that Dervishe's 2018 will was valid, leaving her £1.1 million estate to Dogan.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Kylie Jenner faces fourth household staff lawsuit in seven months as former housekeeper alleges dog bite, pepper spray injury, unpaid overtime and being trapped in a closet
articles.summary: Reality star Kylie Jenner has been sued by a former housekeeper in Los Angeles County Superior Court, the fourth lawsuit from a member of her household
articles.body: Reality star Kylie Jenner has been sued by a former housekeeper in Los Angeles County Superior Court, the fourth lawsuit from a member of her household staff in seven months. Dinora Carolina Cabria Amaya alleges she was trapped in a closet, bitten by a dog and accidentally sprayed in the face with pepper spray from an unsecured canister, and that she was denied fair pay for overtime and travel before being fired. Jenner, 29, who founded Kylie Cosmetics and appears in The Kardashians, faces claims that remain allegations in a court filing, and her attorney has pushed back against them.The lawsuit names Jenner, her company and two staff members over pay, injuries and her firingAccording to USA Today, the complaint was filed on 5 November against Jenner, her company and staff members Laura Dooley and Itzel Sibrian. It alleges workplace violations, disability discrimination, retaliation and wrongful termination. It says that while Amaya worked at Jenner’s properties, from March 2025 until February 2026, she did not receive proper pay, was injured on the job, was discriminated against over those injuries and was fired for raising concerns. The case follows suits filed in April by former housekeepers Angelica Hernandez Vasquez and Juana Delgado Soto, and a June case by a former private chef, all alleging discrimination, harassment and retaliation, among other claims.Amaya was fired after asking about mileage, following a stretch of unpaid overtime, she allegesAmaya says she began in March 2025 on a six-day schedule of eight-hour shifts, reporting to managers Dooley and Sibrian. Almost immediately, she alleges, the defendants’ demands pushed her beyond eight hours a day, yet she was paid the same $40 hourly rate without overtime or double time until May 2025. She raised the issue in a meeting with human resources and says nothing was done to remedy it, though she was then added to payroll and given some overtime and meal break violation pay. She also alleges she was never paid for mileage, vehicle expenses or travel time, despite learning that another housekeeper was compensated. After she asked for mileage in late January, she says she was fired on February 6, less than two weeks later. She alleges the conduct caused lost earnings, lost employment benefits, emotional distress, humiliation and anxiety.A manager allegedly laughed at her while she was locked inside Jenner’s closet and unable to leaveNBC News reports that, on an unspecified date, Dooley told Amaya to enter the closet and gave her the passcode, but she became locked in and was confined against her will for more than an hour. The complaint alleges that when she told Dooley she was trapped and having a panic attack, Dooley laughed and mocked her. Dooley allegedly said that no one was at the house who could let her out, that the password could not be given to anyone else, and that she would simply have to wait.A pepper spray canister and a dog bite left her with injuries, but she says little help followedIn September 2025, Amaya alleges, a canister of pepper spray discharged into her face, leaving ongoing physical impairments that affected her ability to perform certain job duties. On 28 October 2025, she was assigned to clean a doghouse, where a dog allegedly bit her. NBC News notes that the lawsuit does not say whose dog it was. She says she reported the bite to Dooley but received no meaningful help. According to the complaint, the defendants knew she had suffered several injuries and sought medical treatment. It alleges they then removed the housekeeper who had been helping her, made her work alone, assigned heavier and more physically demanding tasks and abruptly changed her schedule and work locations, in what the filing describes as an effort to make her quit.Jenner’s attorney calls the claims meritless while the staff’s lawyer urges workers to speak outJenner’s attorney, Michael Rhodes, told USA Today that the latest cases are being brought by the same lawyer who previously filed claims for her former household staff. He said the lawyer wants to use publicity to extract an unwarranted payday, that Jenner’s team will not be intimidated and that it will defend the meritless cases vigorously. Della Shaker of Shaker Law Group, who represents all four former employees, said in a statement to the same publication that domestic workers do not lose their legal protections by working inside a private home or for a wealthy family. She encouraged anyone who has experienced unpaid wages, discrimination, retaliation or mistreatment to seek confidential legal advice.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'I was told I can't defeat a white American male': Lawmaker Saba Haider
articles.summary: Messages have poured in from \"all corners\" since Saba Haider won the Illinois House of Representatives seat.
articles.body: Messages have poured in from "all corners" since Saba Haider won the Illinois House of Representatives seat. One, received this morning, was from a young Indian woman in international law and politics who had followed the coverage and wanted to learn about her journey. "The response has been amazing. You feel the relief and joy of winning, but also the excitement of getting to work," Haider, who moved to the US at 22, told TOI from her US-home.Politics, she says, was once "completely unimaginable". At Aligarh Muslim University, where she earned a master's in wildlife sciences and an academic gold medal, she studied ecology, with fieldwork at Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary and months in Corbett Tiger Reserve. "It is not easy to study wildlife. I lived in the jungle to study ecology and ecosystems. Not many daughters were allowed to do that," she said."I had no political background, not even distant relatives." Haider won the Democratic primary with more than 60% and the Nov 3 general election with over 70% votes. Illinois, one of the 50 US states, has over 1 crore residents and is best known for its architectural and financial hub Chicago and its association with Abraham Lincoln. Haider will represent the 84th House District in Chicago's western suburbs.Her family hails from Bulandshahr, and she grew up in Ghaziabad before moving to US at 22. She and her husband went on to build a life there and raise their two children. "My husband and I had chosen this country to have and raise our kids... America welcomed us," she told TOI. But the political climate began changing after Donald Trump's election in 2016, a sort of "trigger moment" for her, with increasingly hostile rhetoric around immigrants and discrimination against people who looked like her, which jolted her into action. "I felt America was better than that. I wanted to do something about it, beyond running my business and family." Community engagement and public-health work drew her into local politics.After losing the DuPage County Board in 2022 by a margin of about 1,000 votes, she won in 2024 with over 50% votes, working on public-health initiatives, including on a Crisis Recovery Centre offering mental-health and addiction care.During the Democratic primary in March, a woman voter told Haider she liked her, had read her website and was impressed by her achievements, but would vote for her opponent. "When I asked why, she said, 'I don't think you can win against a white male'," Haider recalls. "To be told that to your face by a voter is heartbreaking." She took a deep breath and kept knocking on doors. Voters, she says, "overwhelmingly saw beyond" her skin colour and Indian origin, instead voting candidates who would "get work done."Talking about the Trump-administration, she said politicians may exploit division and fear, but everyday concerns-medical emergencies, hospital debt, unemployment and poor schooling-remain shared. "The perceived fear of a neighbour does not impact a life directly in any way... voters in the US as well as India are increasingly demanding accountability."To young South Asian women, her message is to look beyond their immediate surroundings. "Young women must seek role models beyond their local ecosystem."Her roots, however, remain in India, where her parents and siblings live. She misses "chai, samosas and jalebis", as well as those walks through foggy winter days in Delhi, from Chandni Chowk to the food lanes near Jama Masjid. "I am incredibly lucky to call America home and to be able to impact lives here, but my roots are strong in India." Asked what she would tell her 20-year-old self at AMU, she said: "Keep doing the work, drown out the noise, ignore the doubts and dare to dream."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Drone activity over U.S. base in Britain prompts security response, U.S. military says
articles.summary: LONDON — Unauthorized drone activity has prompted a security response at an American base in Britain, the U.S. military said Friday.
articles.body: LONDON — Unauthorized drone activity has prompted a security response at an American base in Britain, the U.S. military said Friday. Security forces at Royal Air Force Base Lakenheath in eastern England responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity, but no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure have been affected, the U.S. Air Force in Europe said in a statement. “We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the statement said. The drone incident means that three U.S. bases in the United Kingdom have been affected by threats in recent weeks. Friday’s security response at RAF Lakenheath comes just days after the U.S. moved more than a dozen aircraft from a different base just miles away in eastern England — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat. During the plane exodus, RAF Mildenhall also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second-highest level, which is used when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely. A U.S. official said at the time that the decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive. Several weeks ago, a group of men was detained after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford, roughly 150 miles (240 kilometers) west of Mildenhall and Lakenheath. British authorities linked the plot to Iran, and the U.S. withdrew its bombers that had been stationed there. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war. Other arrests followed, and at least three men have been charged with plotting to attack RAF Fairford. Also this week, a U.S. Army officer assigned to a NATO unit at a military base near Gloucester, England, was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with the suspected terror plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford, also near Gloucester.

articles.title: In a Karnataka village where patients were rushed to hospitals in auto-rickshaws, drivers and residents pooled savings to buy a Rs 12 lakh ambulance; the drivers now offer free emergency transport for two villages
articles.summary: A difficult journey to the hospital became the reason for a remarkable community initiative in Karnataka.
articles.body: A difficult journey to the hospital became the reason for a remarkable community initiative in Karnataka. After repeatedly rushing sick villagers to hospitals in their auto-rickshaws because ambulances were not readily available, a group of drivers decided to find a permanent solution. They pooled their savings, sought help from villagers and donors, and purchased a fully equipped ambulance worth around Rs 12 lakh. Today, the drivers themselves are taking turns to provide free emergency transport to residents of two villages in Bantwal taluk.When auto-rickshaws became the only option during emergenciesIn several parts of rural India, reaching a hospital during a medical emergency can be a challenge, particularly when an ambulance is not readily available. Residents of Kariyangala and Ammunje villages in Karnataka's Bantwal taluk had faced this difficulty on multiple occasions. Whenever someone fell seriously ill or needed urgent medical attention, families sometimes had no choice but to depend on auto-rickshaws to transport patients to hospitals.For the auto-rickshaw drivers, however, these situations were not easy to handle. Their vehicles were not designed to transport patients requiring emergency medical assistance, and the absence of a dedicated ambulance made an already stressful situation more difficult for families. The repeated experiences eventually made the drivers realise that the villages needed a proper ambulance service. Instead of waiting for an outside organisation to address the problem, they decided to take responsibility themselves. The initiative was led by the Navodaya Auto-rickshaw Drivers and Owners Association of Badakabail in Kariyangala village, near Polali.How small contributions turned into a Rs 12 lakh ambulanceWhat makes the initiative particularly noteworthy is how the drivers arranged the money. Rather than depending on a single large donation, the association members contributed through small daily savings. The amount collected from the drivers and owners was combined with financial assistance from villagers and other donors. The group purchased the ambulance for approximately Rs 10 lakh. Another Rs 2 lakh was spent on installing the necessary ambulance equipment in Mysuru, taking the total investment to around Rs 12 lakh.The contribution-based approach allowed people with modest earnings to participate in a project that would benefit the entire community. For the drivers, the ambulance was not simply another vehicle. It was a collective effort to ensure that villagers would not have to depend on ordinary passenger vehicles when someone needed urgent medical attention.The drivers will operate the ambulance themselvesThe association has also worked out how the service will function. There are around 26 auto-rickshaws operating at the Badakabail stand, and the ambulance will be parked near the same stand so that it can be accessed when an emergency arises. Interestingly, the auto-rickshaw drivers themselves will serve as ambulance drivers. This means the community that identified the problem and raised the money will also take responsibility for operating the service.The ambulance will cater to residents of both Kariyangala and Ammunje villages. The service will be provided free of cost, helping families access emergency transportation without having to worry about paying for the journey. By keeping the vehicle close to the auto-rickshaw stand and involving local drivers, the association hopes to make emergency transportation more accessible to people in the surrounding villages.A community that has been contributing beyond this initiativeThe ambulance project is also part of a larger effort by the association to support people in need. Every month, Rs 100 is collected from each auto-rickshaw driver to help underprivileged people. Over time, these contributions have helped the drivers and owners collectively raise more than Rs 4 lakh for various welfare activities. The latest initiative reflects the same spirit of collective responsibility. Each contribution may have been small individually, but together, the drivers, villagers and donors managed to arrange the funds required to purchase and equip an ambulance.For the residents of Kariyangala and Ammunje, the new vehicle represents more than improved transportation. It offers an additional option when a medical emergency strikes, reducing their dependence on auto-rickshaws for journeys to hospitals. The initiative also highlights how local communities can identify everyday problems and work together to address them. The drivers were familiar with the difficulties villagers faced because they had personally been involved in transporting patients during emergencies.Instead of treating those experiences as isolated incidents, they turned them into a reason to act. Their effort is a reminder that meaningful community service does not always begin with large organisations or substantial resources. Sometimes, it starts with a group of people recognising a shared problem and deciding that they can do something about it. For these auto-rickshaw drivers, the goal was simple: ensure that no villager has to depend on an ordinary passenger vehicle when an ambulance is needed.You use AI every day. articles.title: New York has launched a construction-material reuse hub at Brooklyn's Bush Terminal; the year-long pilot will recover and redistribute materials that would otherwise become demolition waste
articles.summary: A building renovation can leave behind more than bricks, timber and metal.
articles.body: A building renovation can leave behind more than bricks, timber and metal. Much of what comes out of a construction site is still usable, yet finding somewhere to store it, sort it and make it available for another project has often been a challenge. New York City is now testing a way to address that gap. A new construction material reuse hub has opened at MADE Bush Terminal in Brooklyn, where discarded and surplus building materials will be collected, organised and made available for reuse, as reported by NYC EDU. The year-long pilot is intended to find out whether a dedicated local facility can make material recovery a more practical part of the city's construction industry.How the Brooklyn construction reuse hub will give discarded building materials a second lifeThe Circular Construction Hub is located at MADE Bush Terminal, a redevelopment site on the waterfront in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. The initiative was announced on 25 August 2026 by the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC), which is working with Brooklyn-based ecological landscaping firm Our Temenos to operate the facility.Rather than treating construction leftovers as waste at the end of a project, the hub will provide a place where selected materials can be brought in, assessed, separated and stored before being offered for another use. The process is expected to include material recovery, sorting, handling and redistribution.The pilot will run for 12 months. During that period, the partners intend to examine how the facility works in practice, including the costs involved in receiving and managing materials and the demand from businesses looking for reclaimed supplies.Construction and demolition waste remains a major challenge for New YorkConstruction and demolition debris makes up a substantial portion of the waste generated across New York City. According to NYCEDC, the sector accounts for approximately 40% of the city's total waste generation.That figure includes materials removed during building renovations, redevelopment and demolition. Some are damaged or unsuitable for further use, but others may retain considerable value. Bricks, timber and other building components can sometimes be recovered instead of being discarded, provided they can be removed, handled and stored appropriately.The difficulty is that conventional construction supply chains are generally organised around purchasing new materials. Reclaimed products, by comparison, can be harder to source in consistent quantities. A contractor may have usable materials available after a project but lack the space or time to find another buyer. At the same time, a different construction business might need those very materials but have no reliable way of locating them.The new Brooklyn facility is intended to address that missing link. By providing a shared location for recovered materials, the pilot will test whether a more organised exchange system can reduce the amount of usable construction waste sent for disposal.Our Temenos takes material reuse to a larger scaleOur Temenos, the organisation selected to run the hub, has experience in ecological landscaping, habitat restoration and low-waste design. Its work has included incorporating reused materials into residential and public green spaces, giving the firm practical experience with the difficulties of sourcing and handling salvaged supplies.Founder Rosemarie Miner described, “As landscape contractors with experience building residential and public green spaces, we had a keen awareness as to why salvage and surplus material use wasn’t scaling. It is part of our work as green infrastructure professionals to solve everyday problems, so we turned that lens back on the supply chain!The new facility will allow the firm to explore that process on a larger scale. Its responsibilities will include managing incoming materials, organising storage and testing how recovered products can be made available for resale or redistribution.Miner has also pointed to the difficulties faced by smaller construction businesses, particularly when supply chains become unpredictable or weather-related delays affect operations. A nearby source of reclaimed materials could offer another option for contractors while helping businesses make better use of resources already available within their communities.The project grew out of a wider search for practical climate solutionsThe partnership between NYCEDC and Our Temenos developed through an initiative called Ideas for Impact. The programme invites businesses, community organisations, academic institutions and other groups to propose projects that could support the city's economic development priorities.The Circular Construction Hub is the first project to receive an award through this process.Its development also follows work NYCEDC began in 2024 with the publication of its Clean and Circular: Design & Construction Guidelines. The document sets out ways to reduce material waste and the carbon emissions associated with building projects, including through deconstruction, material recovery and the use of lower-carbon alternatives.Those guidelines have since been incorporated into several NYCEDC capital projects, including renovation work at MADE Bush Terminal. Experience with their implementation helped identify a practical limitation: encouraging material reuse is difficult without places where recovered products can be handled and stored.Turning Brooklyn's old industrial waterfront into a business hubMADE Bush Terminal is itself part of a broader effort to give an old industrial waterfront site a new purpose. The approximately 20-acre property is being redeveloped into a mixed-use campus for manufacturers, artisans, designers and entrepreneurs.The project includes around 140,000 square feet of industrial workspace, 30,000 square feet for cultural and public activities, and new open spaces. Its development also involves adapting century-old warehouse buildings rather than replacing everything with new construction. That approach has a direct connection with the reuse hub. Retaining existing structures and finding further uses for available materials are both ways of reducing the demand for new resources during redevelopment.Placing the facility within the same industrial campus also gives it access to an area with an established network of businesses and manufacturing activity. The location could help the pilot examine how material recovery fits into the day-to-day needs of contractors, fabricators and other local enterprises. The hub is part of NYCEDC's wider work across the Sunset Park waterfront, a 200-acre district that includes several major industrial properties. These include Brooklyn Army Terminal, South Brooklyn Marine Terminal and the Brooklyn Wholesale Meat Market, alongside MADE Bush Terminal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 4 Nagas killed in sniper attack on Manipur NH
articles.summary: GUWAHATI: Four Tangkhul Naga civilians were shot dead on Friday in a suspected sniper strike by armed men who ambushed two vehicles on NH-202 in Manipur's
articles.body: GUWAHATI: Four Tangkhul Naga civilians were shot dead on Friday in a suspected sniper strike by armed men who ambushed two vehicles on NH-202 in Manipur's Ukhrul, the native district of NSCN (I-M) general secretary Th Muivah. The victims included an elderly woman and her son, and two brothers.The killings came a day after a 42-year-old Kuki woman working in a paddy field along the Senapati-Kangpokpi border was killed in crossfire between gunmen from her community and suspected Naga militants and two men injured. Hours later, a Naga man was wounded in firing by suspected Kuki assailants in Ukhrul. A 48-hour shutdown enforced by Kuki body Committee on Tribal Unity (CoTU) was underway in Kangpokpi against the woman's killing.Manipur outfit blames Kuki narco-terrorists for attackFriday’s ambush, where four Tangkhul Naga civilians were shot dead, took place at New Heaven, along the highway connecting Imphal with Ukhrul, before the victims reached Litan to join a govt-provided security escort. Travel along the Imphal-Ukhrul route requires civilians to join security convoys through a 20km sensitive stretch. It was the second attack at the same location since April 18 when two Naga civilians were killed.The deceased in Friday’s strike were identified as Kapangkhui Raihing and her son Haoleila Raihing, and siblings August Ngalung and Khanmila Ngalung. The Raihings were in one car and the Ngalungs in another.Manipur Police said the attack was carried out by “unknown armed miscreants” and that all four victims suffered fatal bullet injuries, dying on the spot.“Additional security forces comprising Manipur Police, BSF, Army and Assam Rifles have been rushed to the area to reinforce security. Search operations have been launched in and around the area of the incident to trace and apprehend those involved,” the police said in a statement.The latest attack triggered competing allegations and demands. Indigenous People’s Forum alleged that the highway ambush was part of a continuing “war against indigenous people of Manipur” by “Kuki narco-terrorist elements”. The forum sought an impartial probe into the ambush, including into possible collusion by security forces or negligence.Kuki CSO Working Committee, Ukhrul, condemned the attack but denied any community involvement.It warned against collective blame and selective operations in Kuki-Zo areas while demanding time-bound investigations and equal security for all communities. The committee also sought scrutiny of escort arrangements and possible links to a wider conflict involving NSCN factions.Congress legislature party chief Keisham Meghachandra questioned BJP govt’s accountability, saying five people had been killed in 24 hours. Meghachandra also condemned the killings of both Kuki and Naga civilians and said peace could not be achieved without justice and a roadmap to end the conflict.At least 66 people have been killed in Kuki-Naga clashes since Feb.
